subject: 34A3FA09461A48D6B1F6B3D25BBA965F
introduction: Bahá’u’lláh’s Tablet of Wisdom praises the Greek philosophers by name and repeats the tradition, common in Islamic histories, that they learned from the prophets of Israel; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá often told audiences that Socrates journeyed to the Holy Land and returned to teach the unity of God. The guide gathers these statements with his judgment that Greek civilization, for all its beauty, remained material, and ends with letters written for Shoghi Effendi and the Universal House of Justice: there is no historical proof of the journeys, and Bahá’u’lláh says He is quoting “some accounts of the sages”. Here the outside quotations are the philosophers themselves, in Jowett’s Plato and the Oxford Aristotle, with Paul at Athens, who said both that the Greeks “feel after” God and that philosophy is “vain deceit”, and Justin Martyr, who called Socrates a Christian before Christ.
questions: What do the readings admire in the Greek philosophers, and what do they find lacking?
Paul and Justin, both Christians, judged Greek philosophy very differently. Which is nearer the readings?
The tradition that Socrates studied in the Holy Land has no historical support. How do readings 30 to 32 suggest a believer should hold such a statement?
Reading 4 says the intellect is fallible because philosophers disagree. Is disagreement evidence against reason?
What did the philosophers themselves say about the divine, in the passages set here?

outside.why: The Greek philosophers investigated both natural and spiritual phenomena. Aristotle’s first sentence: all men by nature desire to know.
Wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.
Aristotle, “the first teacher”. His own rule as a pupil: while both are dear, piety requires us to honour truth above our friends.
They taught divine and natural philosophy together. Plato likens the good to the sun, the author of visibility in all visible things, and of generation and nourishment and growth.
The ancients held the intellect the chief criterion. For man the life according to reason is best and pleasantest, since reason more than anything else is man.

Socrates’s contribution to the criterion was a doubt about it: I neither know nor think that I know. The reading says the philosophers’ differences show the intellect fallible. Did the best of them know it already?
Aristotle searched the subtleties of reality. His conclusion about God: the divine thought thinks of itself, and its thinking is a thinking on thinking.
Only two have been called “teacher”. The first of them on the first cause: it produces motion as being loved.
Plato, a mere human being, arose with great determination. The soul is in the very likeness of the divine, and immortal.
Plato examined a pupil before accepting him. Socrates called his own teaching midwifery: I look after their souls when they are in labour.
The philosophers’ influence, without the Spirit, has been comparatively small. The Greeks seek after wisdom: but we preach Christ crucified, unto the Greeks foolishness.
Greece founded a material civilization, Christ a spiritual. The world by wisdom knew not God.

The second-century philosopher Justin would not draw the line there: those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists; he meant Socrates. Is the reading’s contrast between Greek and Christian civilization fair to what readings 1 to 8 say of the Greeks?
Greek civilization beautiful but material. Paul’s warning: beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit.
Lycurgus tried to make his people equal. Plutarch gives the reason: the state was overloaded with indigent persons, while its whole wealth had centred upon a very few.
A king who was a philosopher. Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy.
Alexander sought the world and ended with nothing. Marcus Aurelius: Alexander the Macedonian and his groom by death were brought to the same state.
The sages learned from the Prophets. Paul at Athens, quoting their own poets: that they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him.
Philosophers journeyed to Jerusalem in Solomon’s day. There came of all people to hear the wisdom of Solomon, from all kings of the earth.
The Gospel remembers one such traveller, the queen of the south: she came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon.
Socrates learned the unity of God and immortality, and was put to death for it. Men of Athens, I honor and love you; but I shall obey God rather than you.
Socrates taught the Greeks the oneness of God. Paul found at Athens an altar with this inscription, To the Unknown God.
Philosophers change their views after twenty years. Plato’s question about any such account: what is that which always is and has no becoming, and what is always becoming and never is?

“We have no historical proof” of the philosophers’ visits to the Holy Land. Socrates held that the life which is unexamined is not worth living. How do readings 30 to 32 examine the tradition the earlier readings report?

shortfall: Readings 5, 10, 15, 18, 23 to 27, 29, 30 and 32 repeat the tradition of the philosophers’ journeys or concern later schools; the Greek texts placed here are the companions the subject itself supplies.

kings-came-to-hear-the-wisdom-of-solomon.text: And there came of all people to hear the wisdom of Solomon, from all kings of the earth, which had heard of his wisdom

matthew-queen-of-the-south.text: The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: for she came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and, behold, a greater than Solomon is here
